How this book matches your exam. Research check against the Cambridge International AS & A Level Psychology 9990 syllabus:

  • Paper 1 (Approaches, Issues and Debates; 1 hour 30 minutes; 60 marks; 50% of AS, 25% of A Level) tests 12 core studies, three for each of the biological, cognitive, learning and social approaches.
  • The core studies in this book are the biological ones in the syllabus used up to 2027 exams: Dement and Kleitman (1957), Hassett et al. (2008) and Hölzel et al. (2011).
  • Cambridge has published a new reference list for 2028–2030, so check which syllabus year your exam follows.
  • Questions use the command words outline, describe, explain, evaluate and suggest.
  • The marking guides are our own and are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: The Biological Approach: Assumptions and Methods

Key ideas

  • Assumption 1: behaviour, thoughts and feelings are influenced by physiological processes, such as brain activity, hormones and the nervous system.
  • Assumption 2: behaviour can be influenced by genetics and evolution. Some behaviours are innate and adaptive.
  • Typical methods:
  • laboratory experiments;
  • brain scans (MRI, fMRI);
  • physiological measures, such as EEG (brain waves), EOG (eye movements) and EMG (muscle tone);
  • comparative studies with animals.
  • Strengths: the measures are objective and quantitative, and studies are often highly controlled and replicable.
  • Weaknesses: the approach can be reductionist, ignoring thoughts and social context. It may be deterministic. Lab settings may lack ecological validity. Animal findings may not generalise to humans.
  • Key vocabulary:
  • REM sleep: rapid eye movement sleep, linked to dreaming.
  • NREM sleep: non-REM sleep.
  • Grey matter: neuron cell bodies.
  • Sex-typed toys: toys associated with one sex.
  • Neuroplasticity: the brain's ability to change its structure.

Worked examples

Example 1: Outline one assumption of the biological approach. (2 marks) Answer: Behaviour is influenced by physiological processes (1), for example brain activity measured by EEG changes during REM sleep, which is associated with dreaming (1).

Example 2: Explain why an EEG is an objective measure. (2 marks) Answer: It records electrical activity of the brain mechanically (1), so the data do not depend on the researcher's interpretation or the participant's self-report (1).

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark) What does EOG measure? Answer: eye movements.
  2. (1 mark) Name one brain-scanning technique. Answer: MRI / fMRI.
  3. (2 marks) Outline the second assumption of the biological approach. Answer: behaviour is influenced by genes/evolution (1) ; e.g. innate sex differences in toy preference in monkeys (1).
  4. (3 marks) Explain one strength and one weakness of using physiological measures. Answer: strength: objective/quantitative, so comparable and replicable (1 + 1 for explanation) ; weakness: e.g. may not capture subjective experience such as dream content (1).
  5. (3 marks) Explain why the biological approach can be described as reductionist. Answer: it explains complex behaviour in terms of a single level such as brain structures (1) ; it ignores cognitive, social or cultural influences (1) ; example, e.g. explaining toy preference only by hormones (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Describing assumptions without an example.
  2. Confusing EEG and EOG.
  3. Claiming biological = always lab experiments.
  4. Saying "reductionist" without explaining why.
  5. Mixing up REM and NREM.

Quick recall

  1. EEG measures? 2. EMG measures? 3. Two assumptions? 4. One weakness? 5. Grey matter?

Answers: 1) Brain electrical activity. 2) Muscle tone. 3) Physiology; genes/evolution. 4) Reductionism / low ecological validity. 5) Neuron cell bodies.
